K. CULTURAL RESOURCES
Historic Resources
The community of San Jose has a rich historical background, starting from its inception in 1777. A detailed narrative of the history of San Jose and Alviso is included in Appendix D of this report.
In recent years the cultural and historical legacy of San Jose has prompted the investigation of the city and its past in an effort to identify remaining landmarks and preserve them for the future. During 1974 the San Jose Historic Landmarks Commission compiled an Historic Sites Inventory of San Jose. The County of Santa Clara has also compiled an inventory of historic buildings and sites within the County, including some in San Jose. The State of California and the federal government, through the Department of Parks and Recreation and Department of the Interior, respectively, have also designated certain sites in the area as significant, from a historic, cultural, architectural, or archaeological standpoint.
The Historic Sites Table identifies each designated site or structure and identified the agency which has so classified the building or site. (Refer to Table VIII)
Recently there has begun a State-funded survey of San Jose which is investigating the possibility of designating "historic districts" within the city. Such a district would be unique or significant because of their architectural, cultural or historical character and background. The survey was prompted by recent federal legislation which offers substantial tax credits for the rehabilitation of structures in certified historic districts. At present the law only applied to income property, but new legislation may extend the tax credit to all categories of property.
The urban design features and architectural character of the target C.D.B.G. neighborhoods is discussed in the Urban Design portion of this document. The Campus CNRA stands out as a prime candidate for designation as a historic district because of the presence of numerous fine example of late 19th and early 20th century architecture. The Campus neighborhood is also threatened by continued destruction of older structures and their replacement with modern and architecturally incompatible apartment buildings.
Archaeological Resources
The following general discussion of the prehistoric archaeological background of San Jose is repeated from the EIS/EIR on the first three year C.D.B.G. program, published in April 1975.
The resources which constitute the "prehistoric archaeological sites" which are the concern of this element are the cultural remains of the aboriginal peoples who once occupied the San Jose area.
